It and the dead sizes' patch (item 12) were re-based past climb batch 7's `tabulate` rename and re-measured on 2026-09-29, as `reviews/batch-6b-7-conformance.md` finding 7 asked: `reviews/decision-d-diff/rebase-2026-09-29/` (`decision-d.patch`, and `library-e3.patch`, which applies again). The model's lines are the same, 21 out and 29 in; C4's own errors on the compiled checker are 26 as written and 14 with the diff; walk's check passes 40 of 40 with identical values (`reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 2).

### Phase 4. The switch-over

- The natives (`perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md`, R5). The one library has 424 live native bindings on `main` after rung V (425 counted before it): 147 the compiled prelude already binds, 61 with a helper nothing binds yet, 138 that need a new static helper, 78 other (36 methods of native I/O objects, 42 with no compiled analogue). One binding text serves both paths, measured: an `import java` component runs on walk after six small Java patches, 0.1K lines, and the library's `builtinPrimitive` string can name a static helper instead (walk's half measured). Which of the two is the text was item 35: `builtinPrimitive` naming a static helper, the compiled rewrite switched on by the compile command from N1 (P-58, "The natives' one binding text is `builtinPrimitive` naming a static helper (item 35)."). The plan, nine rungs, about three gated batches, before the switch-over and beside phase 3, since they touch walk and the library's binding bodies and not the checker, moving walk onto the helpers one family at a time, each gated by the interpreter suite: N0, the mechanism (1 rung, Java); N1, the 147 bound natives (2, library text only); N2, the 61 with a helper, the 12 wrapping operators bound to the wrapping helpers (1); N3, the 132 new helpers and their 138 bindings (3, Java and library); N4, the I/O objects, a Java-backed writer type and `stdOut` first, since every program's `println` goes through `Writer` (2). On the switch-over day, N5 inside the names batch: the foreign-
- The names: the compiled path reads the interpreter's library, and the compiler's three prelude files are deleted with their tests kept. At least 48 compiler tests are respelled, the reversed wrap spellings of row 348 among them, and rows 381 and 383 close (inventory B1 step 15).

- From the reviews: printing an object with no `asString` overflows the stack once the compiled path reads the one library (`reviews/batch-3-conformance.md`); nothing in the library narrows a number with a check after the prelude's `asZZ32` leaves (`reviews/batch-3.5-4-conformance.md`).
- Rows 476 and 480's probes (`compile-ladder/rung-ranges-zz32/probes/CaseProbeJ.fss`, `probes/skeptic/SkCaseGuardsC.fss`) become gated compiled tests once programs compile against the one library; two status texts retire with the prelude, rung U's callout (`Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:102-109`) and the `case` rule's compiler-world branch (`Functionals.scala:871-874`) (`reviews/batch-7R-conformance.md` finding 3 and "The global questions").
- The compiler prelude's own defects retire with it, each gated. Its range defects, rows 453, 479 and 481: row 450's fix, which row 453's compiled test waited on, is in the one library since climb batch 6.5b's rung E (`413f36ac0`), so that test goes green with the switch-over alone (`reviews/batch-6b-7-conformance.md`, rung O's "Later phases"; `reviews/batch-6.5b-review.md`, Part 3). And its `RR32`, which climb batch 6.5b's rung V measured: row 528, `a = b` over two `RR32` values compiling clean and dying with `java.lang.AbstractMethodError`, because the prelude's `RR32` declares `Equality[\RR32\]` without an `=` (gated by `ProjectFortress/library_tests/XXXRR32EqualityRungV.fss` with its link test); and row 529, `RR32` with `RR32` answering `RR64`, since the prelude's `RR32` declares no arithmetic, order or `MIN` and `MAX` (home 3, though route A, each number type carrying its own algebra, covers it; `reviews/batch-6.5b-review.md`, rung V, standard 1). Row 528's default is the switch-over, by the one-library decision (POSITIONS 2026-09-21, the library route: "from now no declaration goes into the compiler's prelude"); the one prelude line the rung measured, `opr =(self, other:RR32)` in `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:992-994` (`compile-ladder/rung-rr32-sibling/probes/comp/local-fix.patch`), would be an exception only he could grant, and nothing asks for one. When the compiled path takes the one library, the test's two `RR32` bindings of a numeral (`XXXRR32
- Q-walk, the walk half of the numeral switch (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, the numeral switch, 15:18 UTC; `reviews/numeral-switch-judgement.md` section 4.4), in the batch whose step gives walk the checker's static types, or the one after: walk's numeral an `IntLiteral`, Q1's default in rung K's `narrowest` and `bestMatchWithCoercion`, row 387's return conversion, the four natives reading `getInt()`, the fit rule for a numeral too large for `ZZ32`, `IntLiteral`'s missing operators, the coercion pass's symbolic-type bug, row 486's size value; the devices for rows 395 and 511 and `asif`, unless a walk rung after 7b takes them sooner; the three team tests restated (about 5 lines in 3 files) and the library catch-alls' tests, each shown to him. Rows 79, 443, 437's walk half, 486, 395 and 511 are on its line. About 1.5M to 2.5M tokens. That step is R7's second step and is not yet designed; if it is cut or comes late, Q-walk needs option 1's full set then.
- Row 578, for Q-walk (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, Part 3): under walk the object `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic answers a `ZZ32` where its api declares `IntLiteral` (`x + x` prints `0 ZZ32`), since its natives return `FIntLiteral.make`, which normalises to an `Int`; no numeral reaches it while walk's numeral is an `Int`; pinned by `ProjectFortress/tests/IntLiteralValue.fss`, which moves when Q-walk's `FIntLiteral.make` returns an `IntLiteral`.
- Row 579, the switch-over's library work (the same Part 3): against the one library the compiled checker refuses the floor and ceiling brackets of a `ZZ32` or a numeral as an ambiguous coercion and types `round(z)` at `QQ`'s `ZZ`, because `Integral`'s body declares the two brackets and `round` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:702-704`) and its api does not; the device is rung Q's for `ZZ`'s api, `Integral`'s api stating the three and `IntLiteral` its own three; no gated program observes the checker over the one library before the switch-over, so the row is its record.
- After the names, P-68's library rung for row 330: `floor` and `ceiling` on the float types keep the float; the brackets, `round` and `truncate` return the unbounded ℤ, and the library's `truncate` and `round` are tidied to match, with `RR32`'s four sites that climb batch 6.5b's rung V added (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:112`, `:114-116`), gated, the count of interpreter tests whose output changes measured first (R1's line in `PLAN-history.md`).

- From the generic-`distribute` probe (`perf-probes/generic-distribute/REPORT.md` section 7; row 495's family): on the compiled path an object's inherited generic method beside its own plain one dies at the generic arm in the class loader (`IndexOutOfBoundsException` in `readAndExpandGenericThing`), on the base too; with P-151's generic `distribute`, `Generator2` reaches that arm for every pair with no fused overload once the compiled path reads the one library.

Not yet designed as briefs. The record's shape is at least two batches (`coordinator/library-route-judgement.md:37`).

### Phase 5. microGPT compiles

- The model's static types (decision D). As written today, nothing in microGPT passes the checker whatever the storage, because its arrays are unsized in its types (inventory B1 step 17; `reviews/array-design-review.md:13`).
- The array design: row 40's three questions, the element width (`RR32` or `RR64`), and what puts `double[]` under the sized traits (decision A) (inventory B1 step 18, items 15 and 16). The clean list of 2026-09-29 (R6) gives the six forks in the order they need deciding, item 13 below.
- The compiled dispatcher receives the call's static return type, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time is instantiated by the paper's instance rule (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, a type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix; POPL 2019 [R-Method] and [Solve-Step], pp. 11:17-19; `reviews/decisions-review/popl-recheck.md` sections 1.6 and 1.12). Today the code generator reads the arm's static arguments from the value's descriptor (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1484`) and does not pass the return type (`:2048`, "Not sure what to do with return type"). Gated by batch 7b's rung C's expected-failure pair (row 538, `compiler_tests/XXXGenericInstanceUnfixed`). With it the positional rule's restriction can be lifted (the recheck's item 1.3). Walk keeps the value's type as its limit. The paper expects the cost to be "relatively low but nonzero" in the invariant case (pp. 11:24-25; phase 6). A type that holds an opened size, `Array1[\E,0,n#7\]`, is no ground type, and no enclosing instance substitutes for the skolem, so it is completed from the argument's descriptor before it is carried: the paper's calls carry ground types only (pp. 11:16-17; `reviews/array-judgements-popl-check.md`, sections 3 and 7).
4. **Batch N**, the inference rule, its first run landed 2026-09-29 at `3fb0cd8c1` (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/RECORD.md`; review `reviews/batch-N-review.md`); its second run, the numeral switch, retired by the split (P-76): Q-lib landed in batch 8, and Q-walk is phase 4's line.

- F-74 **Walk's numeral stays an `Int` until walk has the checker's static types, since without them a list of numerals and a generic's static argument take their types from the values.** It is P-76's walk half; F-79 is the library half. With walk's numeral an `IntLiteral`, the library loads and both microGPT checks keep their values, but 24 passing interpreter tests fail: 6 by design, 3 of them team tests that assert a `ZZ32`; 9 for want of static types (rows 364, 510); and 9 walk gaps. A size below 2^31 used as a value is an `Int` too (row 486; F-140). Detail: `reviews/numeral-switch-judgement.md` section 3.
- F-79 **The one library's numeral type is the compiler library's `IntLiteral`, a sibling under `Number` that each integer type, `QQ`, `RR64` and `AnyIntegral` convert from.** It builds P-76's library half. It declares `Integral[\I\]`'s members, `zero` and `one` itself, since `Integral`'s do not apply to a sibling numeral, even with coercion. Each integer type states its comparisons, `CMP`, `MAXNUM`, `MINNUM` and `^` with an `IntLiteral`, which would otherwise tie. `(3).minimum` is refused (row 581). Gated by `tests/IntegerOrderNumerals.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-numeral-library/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 6.

# Fortress gap ledger

The gap ledger records, one claim to a row, where the revival's tree departs from Fortress as its specification and the team's papers describe it: what fails, what works that a source doubted, and wha

Read a row with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'ledger:N'`, and find rows with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'ledger-find:WORDS'`; do not read this file whole. Wri

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number 

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.

===== 11839 2026-09-29T13:58:02.218Z assistant
You're close. Three corrections, then why `Any` isn't just the status quo.

**`Any` and `Bottom` are opposite ends.**
- `Any` is the top: every type sits below it, and every value in Fortress belongs to it.
- `Bottom` is the bottom: it sits below every type and has no values at all. It's the type of an expression that never returns a value, such as `throw`.
- The question in item 3 is only about the top. When a generic declaration writes `[\T\]` with no bound, what may `T` be?

**What `Object` is in Fortress.** It isn't Scala's `object` keyword, although Fortress has a similar keyword:
- A Fortress `object` declaration makes values. Without parameters it's a singleton, like Scala's `object`. With parameters, like `object Just[\T\](x: T)`, it's a constructor, much like a Scala case class. So your memory connects the right things.
- The type `Object` is the supertype of every value those declarations make.
- There are no Java-style primitives at the language level. `ZZ32`, `RR64` and `String` are all under `Object`. The unboxed `double` is only how the compiler may store an `RR64`.

**What `Any` has that `Object` doesn't:** tuples like `(ZZ32, ZZ32)`, functions like `ZZ32 -> ZZ32`, and the empty tuple `()`. In Fortress these are not objects. The 2012 Types chapter says the same: `Any` is the top, and `Object` excludes function types.

**Why `Any` isn't just the status quo:**
- The library's own design needs it. A two-dimensional array is indexed by a pair: `Array[\RR64, (ZZ32, ZZ32)\]`. A list of pairs is `List[\(K, V)\]`. Under `Object`, every generic container instantiated at a tuple would be refused. That was measured at 163 refusals, most of them tuple index types, including the arrays microGPT uses.
- The draft's sentence saying `Object` dates from 2008 to 2010, before the library instantiated generics at tuples everywhere. The 2012 Types chapter makes `Any` the top.
- The compile path currently writes `Object` for an empty bound (row 412), which is why it refuses generics at tuple types today. That divergence goes away at the switch-over.

So the choice is between the draft's 2008 wording and what the library needs and the designers' later text says. Option 1 writes `Any` into the specification with a callout recording that the draft said `Object`.

### 4.2 The walk half meets the limit Pavol already accepted on 2026-09-29

R7 (POSITIONS 2026-09-29, walk's run-time choice of coercions): walk has no static types, so it chooses a coercion on the value where the compiled path resolves it statically; accepted as the interpreter's limit, "one now and two after the switch", walk to be matched once the checker runs on interpreter programs after the switch-over and walk takes the static coercions the checker inserts.

The second group of section 3 is the same limit under another name. `<|1, 2, 3|>` at a `List[\ZZ32\]` parameter is typed by the checker from the parameter; walk builds it from the values and gets `List[\IntLiteral\]`. `getDefault(0, 0, 0)` at an instance walk built from `ZZ32` values gets `(Int, Int, Int)`, into which a numeral does not convert. When walk takes the checker's static arguments and coercions, each of these is settled by the same insertion R7 waits for, with nothing built for it in walk. Building it now, as option 1 asks (row 364's repair beside the devices), writes into walk's inference from values an approximation of static typing that the switch-over then replaces, and by the probe's own reading still does not match the checker. That is work the goal does not need: microGPT's values are unchanged under the switch, its static types are concrete, and rows 79, 443, 454 and 437 are agreement rows between walk and the compiled path, on no path to microGPT compiled.

So the walk half of rung Q waits, for the same reason and to the same point as R7's second step. This keeps the decision (walk switches to `IntLiteral`) and moves its date, on evidence he did not have on 2026-09-27.

**The library rung (call it Q-lib), in batch 8.** Library and glue only, no evaluator file.

As an object, `IntLiteral` excludes `QQ` under walk (row 484's condition) and `XXXextendIntLiteral` stays an expected failure.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).

93:We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
coercion from it.
\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
that \library\ give a numeral.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.}


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
